chapter_theme: Neythal on the Pandya's shore: the heroine wastes in the shore lord's absence (49, 53, 58), turns from him to the stork that saw his oath (50), sends his envoy-bird away (51), recalls the drying-ground where he lied and took her beauty (54, 56), faces the mother's confinement that ends the night meetings (52, 59), is warned her bangles will slip if he leaves unembraced (55), and sees her pallor lift as his chariot comes (60).

49.reading: The heroine bids someone go and tell the lord of the cool sea, where ships ply over the great waves and heaps of prawns lie noisily piled, how she has wasted away with love-sickness, and not to spare him the telling.
49.nuance: Line 3's பாவாரம் சேர்ப்பதற்கு is obscure; the sense needs சேர்ப்பற்கு, 'to the shore lord', as in 51 and 52, and ஓவா கலந்தார்க்கு (to the one who joined without ceasing) is read with it. The ships that never stop plying are set beside a man who has stopped coming.

thinai_evidence.note: the cold sea with its ships and prawn heaps

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the one told to speak (உரையாய்) is unnamed and taken to be the friend

50.reading: The heroine says she will not speak to the lord of the long sea, nor even tell the anril on the palmyra of close-folded fronds, but bids the young broad-footed stork that feeds in the shore grove, which saw him swear his hard oath, to listen.
50.nuance: She passes over the anril, the bird of paired love, which would only mirror her loss, and chooses the stork because it saw the oath: the bird is called as a witness, not a comforter. The poem ends on கேள், so what she tells it is left unsaid.

thinai_evidence.note: the long sea, the shore grove's stork and the palmyra

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the heroine turns from the shore lord and the anril to the stork, the witness of his oath, as the one she addresses

51.reading: Turning to the woman whose eyes are like the sapphire-blue neythal flower, the speaker tells the bird of humble words, which came as envoy for the lord of the clear sea who enjoyed her beauty and went his way, to fly off.
51.nuance: The words தூதொடு வந்த பணிமொழி are the ones Natrinai 167 gives the shore lord's bard: the go-between refused at the door has become a bird. The gap in line 2 hides what the lord did after enjoying her beauty.

thinai_evidence.note: the neythal flower and the shore lord

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; line 1 addresses the heroine and line 4 the envoy bird, which is sent away; the friend is taken as speaker

52.reading: The speaker says the mother too has now kept the girl indoors and asks what they can do, and whether she should not tell the lord of the long backwater, who left without a thought for the one she addresses, the blame they have come to bear.
52.nuance: இல்கடிந்தாள் is the mother's confinement of the girl; with the meetings ended, telling the man of the blame is the friend's way of pressing him to marry.

thinai_evidence.note: the punnai grove and the long backwater

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; taken as the friend speaking to the heroine; புக்கருந்தும் (who enters the punnai grove and feeds) may instead mark the one addressed as a shore bird

53.reading: The heroine asks her friend whether he who left her in the long grove, where crabs move over the dune overrun by adumbu creeper, will not stay away long, and whether the lord of that shore, where heaps of reeking fish are carried off, will not come to be one with them.
53.nuance: நீடார் can be 'will not delay' or 'did not stay'; read as the first, the poem is hope against the fact of his leaving, which is why it is waiting rather than lament.

thinai_evidence.note: crab, adumbu creeper and drying fish of the shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; தோழி in line 4 names the addressee

54.reading: The heroine recalls how she sat in the punnai grove keeping birds off the prawns her brothers had brought to dry, and asks how she can now see the shore lord who lied to her, spoke fine words and enjoyed her beauty.
54.nuance: Near miss for ullurai: the guarded catch and the stolen beauty sit side by side, but no thief-bird is named, so only one pair (her kin's catch to her own beauty) can be drawn; in 56 the bird is named and the image holds.

thinai_evidence.note: the drying prawns and the punnai grove

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; no addressee is named; the friend is assumed

55.reading: The friend tells the girl with eyes like fighting carp that the cool shore lord of the winding backwater, where herons gather at the meeting waters, laughed and played his teasing game by himself, and that if he leaves without embracing her, the bangles will not stay on either of her hands.
55.nuance: அசதி தனியாடி: his play is a game he plays alone, light to him, while for her the bare chance of his leaving unembraced is enough to loosen the bangles.

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the vocative கண்ணினாய் makes the heroine the addressee and the friend the speaker

56.reading: The heroine says that while she stayed blameless, driving off the birds that snatch the strong fish her kin had brought home across the foaming tide, the shore lord of the flowered backwater took his pleasure and consumed her beauty.
56.nuance: She guarded the catch against the small thieves and lost the greater thing to the man; புகரில்லேம் insists the fault was not hers.

thinai_evidence.note: tide, fish and backwater of the shore

comparisons.tenor: the shore lord taking the beauty her family kept

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi

ullurai.tenor: the shore lord and the heroine's beauty

pairs.situation: the shore lord takes what is not his, her beauty
that beauty was her family's charge, kept for them
she watched against the small thieves and missed the one that mattered

ullurai.speaker_fit: the heroine uses her own task on the shore drying-ground, a thing she knows (porul 7.26)

57.reading: The lord of the cool sea, where the curve-beaked anril joined with its mate calls to its kin from the palmyra of cuttable fronds, is set at the hour when the reeking waves beat at the courtyard reached by swimming the moonlit winding backwater; the verse names the hour but not what happens in it.
57.nuance: The four lines have no finite verb. Read as a night meeting, the man swims the backwater to the courtyard while the paired anril calls; the anril calling its mate could carry iraicchi, but with the stated sense unfixed the deletion test cannot be run, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the anril on the palmyra by the cold sea

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai and the verse has no main verb; speaker and addressee are a guess

58.reading: The heroine says that if she sits thinking of the lord of the unreachable water, where heaps of fish struck by sharks swirl in the backwater and the tide that flings up prawns roars, the bangles on her forearm will not hold.
58.nuance: Every creature on his shore strikes or is struck (சுறா எறி, இறா எறி), and the tide roars; against that the loss is quiet: thinking of him alone is enough to loosen the bangles.

thinai_evidence.note: shark, prawn and tide of the backwater

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; no addressee is named; the friend is assumed

59.reading: The friend says that the mother, asking who the young man is who slips through the narrow gap to the soft-spoken girl with the gaze of a young deer, the lord of the cool ford where the heron lays its eggs in the thaazhai, has blocked the gap and shut the door.
59.nuance: நூழை and புழை are the small gaps of the fence by which he came; with the door barred the night meetings are over, and only marriage is left.

thinai_evidence.note: the heron nesting in the thaazhai of the ford

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the girl and the shore lord are both in the third person, and the report of the shut door is taken as addressed to him, to press for marriage

iraicchi.act: the heron lays its eggs and nests in the thaazhai on his shore
iraicchi.sense: the lord of a shore where even the heron settles to breed has yet to make a home with the girl, and the shut door says he must now do it

60.reading: The friend tells the heroine, her flower-creeper, that her golden pallor is gone, for here is the chariot of the man of the bright garland, who has seen the backs of fleeing kings, coming near to join her and scattering the herons of the Pandya's Korkai.
60.nuance: கூடல் is both 'union' and the Pandya's city, so the chariot comes at once to Koodal and to their meeting; the war epithet of the man who saw kings' backs turns the lover's return into a victor's.

thinai_evidence.note: the herons of the Korkai shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; பூங்கொடி addresses the heroine

links.note: Kuruntokai 25: no one was there but the thief and a heron watching for aaral fish on the day he took her, so what can she do if he lies. Kainnilai 50: she will tell neither him nor the anril, only the stork of the grove that saw his hard oath.
links.teaches: The heron that in Kuruntokai only proves how alone the heroine was becomes, in the venba, the one hearer she trusts with the broken oath, so the bird witness of kalavu moves from a sign of her helplessness to the only court left to her.

links.note: Ainthinai Ezhupathu 62: does the heron of the grove not know his cruelty, though it saw him turn graceless? Kainnilai 50: the stork of the grove, which saw his harsh oath, is the one she bids listen.
links.teaches: The two shore venbas value the same bird witness in opposite ways, reproached for seeing and not knowing once the oath is broken, confided in because it saw while she still hopes the oath can be held, so the witness's worth follows the stage of her trust.

links.note: Natrinai 167: the friend refuses the bard who came with the shore lord's message (துறைவன் தூதொடும் வந்த ... பணி மொழி). Kainnilai 51 uses the same words for a bird (தூதொடு வந்த பணிமொழிப் புள்ளே) and tells it to fly off.
links.teaches: The formula that names the bard refused at the door is given in the venba to a bird, showing the short form compressing the social scene of வாயில் மறுத்தல் into a creature of the shore while keeping the old wording.

links.note: Akananuru 20: the friend, with the man listening unseen, says that on the town women's talk of a chariot on the dunes the mother has forbidden their shore play (அன்னை கடிகொண்டனளே). Kainnilai 52: the mother has kept the girl in (அன்னையும் இல்கடிந்தாள்), and the speaker asks whether to tell the man of the blame.
links.teaches: The long poem lets the man overhear the mother's ban, while the venba weighs telling him outright, so the pair shows the ban as the friend's lever for marriage, worked by indirection in one and nearly by open message in the other.

links.note: Kuruntokai 320: on the dune of drying fish and prawns she has not even one day's laughter with the shore lord to be blamed for, yet the town gossips. Kainnilai 54: on the same drying-ground he lied to her and enjoyed her beauty. On a plain reading one heroine denies what the other confesses.
links.teaches: The prawn-drying ground serves one heroine as the scene of an innocence the town will not credit and another as the scene of her seduction, so the stock place of neythal kalavu could carry either a defence before the town or an accusation of the lover.

links.note: Akananuru 20: the friend recalls chasing birds from her father's drying fish (எந்தை தந்த கொழுமீன் உணங்கல் படுபுள் ஓப்பி) among the shore pastimes now forbidden. Kainnilai 56: while driving the birds from the fish her kin brought (எமர் தந்த ... வன்மீன் கவரும்புள் ஓப்பின்), the shore lord took her beauty.
links.teaches: The same chore, keeping birds off the family's catch, is innocent play in the Akananuru list and the very hour of the theft in the venba, which explains why the mother's ban in the long poem falls on just those shore tasks.

links.note: Natrinai 138: the lord of the cool ford where the white heron lays its eggs (வெண் குருகு ஈனும் தண்ணம் துறைவன்) is now known to the old town. Kainnilai 59: the lord of the cool ford where the heron lays its eggs in the thaazhai (குருகுஈனும் தண்ணந் துறைவனை) is now known to the mother, who shuts the door.
links.teaches: The epithet of the nesting heron frames in both poems the moment the secret becomes known, to the town in one and the mother in the other, which supports reading the breeding heron as a call for the man to set up house now that kalavu is over.

links.note: Akananuru 315: the mother who saw the girl grow and suspected, yet did not shut her in (செறியேன்), mourns her elopement. Kainnilai 59: the mother, seeing the young man come through the gap, at once blocks it and shuts the door.
links.teaches: The confinement one mother blames herself for omitting is done at first sight by the other, and the friend reports it as the pressure that forces marriage, so the pair shows the mother's guard as the hinge between the two endings of kalavu, marriage and flight.

links.note: Kural 1157: do the bangles slipping from her wrist not already proclaim that the shore lord has left? Kainnilai 55: if the shore lord leaves without embracing her, the bangles will not stay on either hand.
links.teaches: The venba states as a condition what the couplet packs into a past tense, so it supports reading the Kural's 'has left' as anticipatory: the bangles slip at the mere prospect of the shore lord going.

links.note: Kural 1262: if she forgets him today her beauty will leave and her bangles slip. Kainnilai 58: if she sits thinking of him, her bangles will not hold. On a plain reading forgetting ruins her in one and remembering in the other.
links.teaches: The couplet makes memory the thing that keeps her body whole and the venba makes memory the thing that wastes it, so together they show the bangle as a sign the two traditions could hang on either side of remembering the absent man.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 200: the lord of the golden chariot has come, her bangles fit again and they can laugh at the pallor. Kainnilai 60: her golden pallor is gone, for here is the chariot of the man who saw the backs of fleeing kings, nearing Koodal.
links.teaches: Both mark the end of pallor by the chariot's arrival, but the venba arms the returning lover with a victor's epithet and the Pandya's Korkai and Koodal, showing a late akam poem borrowing puram glory to make homecoming a triumph.

source_issues: 49-60: the source heads these verses பாலை; the work's order and the shore scenes make them நெய்தல், as the colophon field already gives.
49 line 3: பாவாரம் சேர்ப்பதற்கு is likely corrupt; the sense wants சேர்ப்பற்கு, 'to the shore lord'.
51 line 2: part of the line is lost (dots in the source), between உண்டிறந்து and ம்மருளோ.
57: the four lines have no finite verb; a line may be missing or the verse is a fragment.
